News broke that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with someone who is an alleged Chinese spy. That's a major problem considering how vehemently the U.S. government has fought to keep Nvidia's cutting-edge technology out of China's hands. This has caused Nvidia's stock to sell off over the past few days, compounding the fact that it was already declining before this story broke. The reality is that the broader stock market believes AI spending has gone too far and is no longer willing to fully value companies in this sector. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » With some other relationships coming to light and Huang resigning on Nov. 12, Nvidia is entering a new paradigm. Those are two negative forces working against Nvidia stock, which is why it's down 30% from its all-time high. The question is, should you sit this one out or buy more? Here's what I'm doing. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images. The biggest question investors must ask themselves is whether anything has changed inside Nvidia's business. I think the answer to that is no. The AI build-out is still going strong, and several AI hyperscalers have already indicated that 2027's build-out costs will be greater than in 2026. In fact, Nvidia gave guidance that it expects data center capital expenditures by the big five AI hyperscalers to reach $1.3 trillion in 2027, up from nearly $800 billion in 2026. This is projected to lead to 70% revenue growth next year, which is far faster than the market is currently pricing into the stock. The biggest question is what Nvidia will look like without Huang. If the board can identify a suitable long-term replacement, then there's nothing to worry about. However, if the company faces some government-led investigations about what's going on with its business in China through intermediaries, this could be a huge problem for Nvidia. Furthermore, future product development could be an issue, as Huang is viewed as a visionary in his field. There are still many key pieces within the Nvidia organization that can keep the ship on course. I still think the company is in a great position to dominate regardless of who is in the leadership position, but not anyone can run Nvidia. While CFO Colette Kress is taking over as interim CEO, investors should be wary only if she's named the full-time replacement. CEOs with finance backgrounds have harmed many tech companies; just look at what happened with Intel and IBM. If Nvidia's board doesn't learn that lesson, its future could be in jeopardy. However, I have faith that the board will make the right decision. With the most recent sell-off, now is also one of the best times in recent memory to buy the stock. After the sell-off, Nvidia trades for just 21 times earnings. That's significant because it now prices Nvidia at a cheaper level than the S&P 500, which trades at 22.4 times earnings. That's an amazing stat, especially considering that Nvidia's growth is expected to be 70% next year. When next year's earnings projections are used to price the stock, it trades for just 10.6 times next year's earnings. That's just an absurdly low price tag for a company positioned to capitalize on the AI build-out, regardless of who leads it. As a result, I think Nvidia is still a strong buy today. With how cheap the stock has gotten due to the sell-off, there are few better options available in the stock market than Nvidia. While it may take a bit for the stock to regain its swagger, I think it will come with time. There have been many companies that have recovered from failures or scandals, and I believe that Nvidia will be among them in the next few months. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock was plummeting this past Thursday, down about 5% in morning trading after CEO Jensen Huang abruptly resigned following reports in The New York Times of extramarital affairs. The S&P 500, Dow Jones Industrial Average, and the Nasdaq Composite were all down on Nov. 12, but all by less than 1% in morning trading, as the move was likely already priced in by investors. Nvidia stock is down about 11% over the past five days and 29% over the past month. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » It is an unprecedented development at the world's second-largest company, one that may leave many investors wondering what the next steps are. One of Huang's affairs was with a Chinese businesswoman who was reportedly recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information on Nvidia. It led the Nvidia board to conduct an investigation into the matter. The New York Times also reported on Nov. 11 that Huang had an affair with an Nvidia employee. Huang apologized on Nov. 8, stating in a letter to employees: "I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." Four days later, on Nov. 12, Huang resigned from the company that he co-founded in 1993 and has led as CEO for 33 years. He built Nvidia into the largest company in the world in November 2024. It is currently second only to Apple, with a market capitalization of $4 trillion. Nvidia, which makes graphics processing units (GPUs) for AI data centers, became the driving force in the AI boom and Huang became the face of the AI revolution. Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer, was named the interim CEO, effective immediately. "The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, chair of the Nvidia board, said. Kress has been with Nvidia since 2013 when she joined as CFO. "We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers, and shareholders," Kress said. The resignation of the CEO of one of the largest public companies in the world is not unprecedented, but rarely, if ever, have the markets seen such an abrupt exit at a massive company over personal conduct and not due to performance issues or as part of a planned succession. While there have been other personal conduct ousters among CEOs, none of them in recent history have been at a company as large, as influential, and as important to the stock market as Nvidia. In that sense, it is somewhat uncharted territory. But the key for investors is not to make any rash moves and maintain a long-term investing mindset. The first step should be to pore over the various Wall Street analysts' reports on Nvidia following the transition. In recent days, Nvidia stock has received a slew of price target downgrades. RBC Capital recently lowered its target by $100 to $230 per share but maintained its buy rating. Cantor Fitzgerald also lowered it by $100 to $250 per share but kept a buy rating. Others, like Baird and Keybanc, lowered Nvidia's rating from buy to hold or neutral, and reduced its price target. Overall, Nvidia stock has a median price target of $262 per share, which would suggest 57% upside over the next 12 months -- and this includes recently updated projections. Further, 28 analysts still rate it as a buy, with only 8 calling it a hold, and 0 rating it as a sell. Next, investors should tune in for Nvidia's third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, Nov. 17, after the market closes. Nvidia is expected to generate $108 billion in revenue in its Q3. That would be up 12% from Q2 and 89% year-over-year. While robust, it is slightly slower growth than in Q2. The consensus among analysts is about $109.4 billion in revenue. But investors should also be watching for news on the leadership transition, the hiring of a new CEO, any news of the Huang investigation, and anything else that can provide some visibility into where the company is headed following this major and abrupt transition. Finally, investors should take note that Nvidia stock is trading at a valuation it has not seen in years. It is trading at just 21 times earnings and 11 times forward earnings. The last time its P/E ratio was this low was in 2019. Since that time in 2019, Nvidia stock has grown about 3,200%. Also, its five-year PEG ratio, which gauges its valuation relative to its long-term earnings expectations, is just 0.22. Anything under 1.0 is considered a value, so the 0.22 PEG ratio would suggest it is a value relative to its earnings potential. While the upheaval is concerning and worth a cautious eye, Nvidia remains the dominant player in its field, and its AI chips sit at the center of the AI boom and massive hyperscaler build-out. title: Espionage Fears And Executive Scandal Trigger NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Freefall, Rocking The Broader AI Trade - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 15, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis U.S. intelligence officials’ suspicions about a former chip-industry executive’s alleged ties to Chinese espionage have landed at the center of one of the biggest corporate implosions in recent memory. Jensen Huang, who built NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) into a multi-trillion-dollar artificial intelligence powerhouse, abruptly stepped down as president and CEO with immediate effect following a cascade of personal revelations. The departure came after Huang publicly acknowledged marital infidelity, with reports identifying his companion as Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, which is itself an NVIDIA customer. American intelligence officials have reportedly flagged Alice Huang, who shares no family relation with Jensen, as a suspected spy for China, adding a national security dimension to what began as a personal scandal. Separate reports also emerged of an affair between Huang and an NVIDIA executive, surfacing in the days immediately preceding his resignation and compounding the reputational damage to the company. NVDA shares plunged sharply in the wake of the announcement, and the fallout has spread across the AI sector as questions mount over the pace of the industry’s infrastructure buildout. Markets were already under pressure before the NVIDIA shock, as October consumer price data came in hotter than expected and annual producer inflation climbed to its highest level in roughly four years. Against that backdrop, Anthropic’s planned November 19 IPO is drawing attention as a potential counterweight, with analysts noting that investors appear to be rotating out of certain AI positions ahead of the listing. Anthropic’s S-1 filing has been closely scrutinized, with analysis suggesting the document strengthens the growth argument for Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO), whose AI chip business stands to benefit from Anthropic’s escalating rivalry with NVIDIA. Elsewhere, monday.com (NASDAQ: MNDY) is attracting attention from analysts who argue that a combination of share buybacks and an accelerating AI strategy could position the company for a meaningful recovery. Consumer spending will come into sharper focus in the coming days as major retailers begin reporting quarterly results, offering a read on household demand heading into the critical holiday season. Investors navigating an unusually volatile stretch will also be watching for previews of the top five stocks analysts favor heading into December, as portfolio positioning shifts across both tech and broader equity markets. title: Bessent calls for ‘dramatic shakeup’ at Nvidia, urges outside CEO - CNBC

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a “dramatic shakeup” at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings. Bessent said Nvidia’s board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant’s compliance with U.S. export controls. “I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” Bessent said in an interview on Fox News. The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump’s handling of the matter. Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains “complete confidence” in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter. Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO. Bessent’s remarks came two days after he told CNBC’s “Squawk Box” that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government’s export blacklist for months. title: Nvidia Earnings Preview: Can AI Growth Stabilize NVDA Stock After Jensen Huang’s Resignation? - Markets.com
content: Nvidia’s upcoming earnings report will test whether extraordinary AI chip growth can restore confidence in NVDA stock following the sudden resignation of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang. The company is expected to report another quarter of rapid revenue growth, driven by Blackwell accelerators, networking products and the early deployment of its Vera Rubin platform. However, investors will also be assessing leadership continuity, declining gross margins, China restrictions and the sustainability of record AI infrastructure spending. Nvidia will announce its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. Pacific Time, or 4:20 p.m. Eastern Time. For investors in the UAE, the results are expected at approximately 1:20 a.m. GST on Wednesday, November 18. The earnings call will begin about 40 minutes later at 2 p.m. Pacific Time. The quarter ended on October 25, 2026. Nvidia will publish written commentary from interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress immediately after releasing the results. Wall Street expects Nvidia to report approximately $109.3 billion to $109.4 billion in quarterly revenue, slightly above the company’s guidance midpoint of $108 billion. Analysts also forecast net income of approximately $60.9 billion, while one widely cited estimate places non-GAAP earnings at roughly $2.45 per share. Meeting the consensus estimate would represent sequential revenue growth of approximately 14% and year-over-year growth of roughly 90%. Nvidia’s official guidance calls for revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, meaning a reported figure between approximately $105.8 billion and $110.2 billion would fall within the company’s stated range. Data Center revenue is once again expected to dominate the results. Visible Alpha estimates that the division generated approximately $101.8 billion during the quarter, although individual analyst forecasts range from $99.7 billion to $110.8 billion. The wide range reflects uncertainty over product availability, customer deployment schedules and the transition between Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin architectures. During the previous quarter, Data Center revenue reached $89 billion, rising 18% sequentially and 117% from the same period a year earlier. Total company revenue increased 106% year over year to $96.2 billion. Investors will want confirmation that spending by Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, Oracle and newer AI cloud providers remains strong despite concerns about rising debt and the financial returns generated by AI infrastructure. A significant earnings beat would suggest that demand continues to exceed Nvidia’s ability to supply advanced systems. A weaker result could reinforce concerns that hyperscalers are becoming more selective about new data-center commitments. Product-mix commentary may be more important than the headline revenue figure. Analysts expect Nvidia’s Blackwell platform to generate approximately $148.9 billion in fiscal 2027, up from around $98 billion in the previous year. Blackwell remains a major contributor, but customers are already shifting attention toward the newer Vera Rubin architecture. Visible Alpha’s consensus estimate places third-quarter Rubin-related revenue at approximately $48.5 billion, although forecasts range from $37.6 billion to $65.5 billion. The unusually wide range shows how difficult it is to estimate the timing of large AI system deliveries. Nvidia previously said Vera Rubin had entered full production, with systems operating at partners including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle, CoreWeave and Nebius. The company’s fourth-quarter guidance will therefore be critical. Investors will look for evidence that Rubin supply is increasing quickly enough to support another acceleration in Data Center growth. Nvidia guided for a third-quarter gross margin of 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points, compared with 75% in the previous quarter. The expected decline reflects higher memory costs, the complexity of complete rack-scale systems and expenses associated with introducing new products. Margins could face additional pressure in the fourth quarter. Some analyst models expect gross margin to fall toward 71% to 72% before recovering to approximately 72% to 73% during fiscal 2028. A revenue beat accompanied by weak margins might not be enough to stabilize NVDA stock. Investors will want evidence that Nvidia can maintain pricing power as the product mix shifts toward larger systems that include GPUs, CPUs, networking equipment, cooling and software. Conversely, a gross margin above 74% would suggest that strong demand and favorable pricing are offsetting higher component and deployment costs. This earnings report will be Nvidia’s first major investor event since Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and board member on November 12. Nvidia appointed Kress as interim CEO while she continues serving as CFO. The board has begun searching for a permanent successor and said it will consider both internal and external candidates. Kress joined Nvidia in 2013 and has overseen its financial organization throughout the company’s transformation from a gaming-chip manufacturer into the dominant provider of AI computing infrastructure. The board has said it expects Nvidia’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Nevertheless, Huang’s departure creates significant key-person risk. He played an unusually central role in Nvidia’s product strategy, customer relationships and public identity. Investors will listen closely for details about the CEO search, management responsibilities and whether the leadership transition could affect Rubin’s deployment or longer-term product development. Nvidia’s third-quarter forecast assumed no Data Center compute revenue from China. US export restrictions continue to limit the company’s ability to sell its most advanced AI chips in the country. Chinese competitors are also developing domestic accelerators, potentially reducing Nvidia’s long-term market opportunity even if export rules eventually become less restrictive. Any improvement in China access could provide upside to future revenue estimates. However, tighter restrictions or accelerating domestic competition would make Nvidia even more dependent on US hyperscalers, sovereign AI projects and customers in other international markets. Nvidia shares closed Friday near $163 after falling approximately 12% during the week. The stock is now more than 30% below its October record high. Options pricing indicates that traders expect an approximately 8% move in either direction by the end of earnings week. Based on Friday’s closing price, that could push Nvidia above $176 following a positive report or below $150 after a disappointment. Nvidia’s underlying AI business remains exceptionally strong, but this report carries more uncertainty than recent quarters. A convincing earnings beat and strong guidance could demonstrate that customer demand and the product roadmap remain intact without Huang. Anything less may leave leadership risk, margin pressure and AI spending concerns at the center of the NVDA stock outlook. Keep up with the latest price movements and market developments. As the market digested the unfolding drama, at least 10 analysts downgraded their Buy rating on the stock to Hold. The analyst, who slapped a Market Perform rating on the stock with a $200 price target, called into question the ability of any new CEO to truly fill Jensen's shoes "given how tightly he managed the direction of the business and its relationships with customers, suppliers, employees, and the broader industry ecosystem." Until the board announced Huang's resignation, Wall Street had long grappled with Nvidia's one-man risk: a larger-than-life CEO whose role had come to seem irreplaceable to the company and the broader AI market. "How can you have the world's most valuable company and no kind of succession plan, not even anyone being groomed with 60 people reporting to Jensen?" former Medtronic CEO Bill George told Yahoo Finance on Friday. Soon, investors may not be able to see him sell it. Nvidia's (NVDA) board accepted Huang's resignation on Nov. 11. He walks away from about $108 million in unvested stock awards, pocket change next to the roughly 812 million shares he keeps, worth about $132 billion at Friday's close. That makes him Nvidia's largest individual owner. When an insider sells, Wall Street sometimes reads it as a vote of no confidence in the company. When the founder of the world's most important AI chipmaker sells, the whole market can follow. "This is no doubt an overhang on the trade for the foreseeable future," Liz Thomas, SoFi's chief market strategist, told Yahoo Finance on Thursday. Investors are already voting. Nvidia stock closed Friday at its lowest level since July 2025, about 32% below its Oct. 6 record. Legally, Huang can sell now. For three months after leaving, he still counts as a company insider, so any big sale needs a public notice filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The legal cap on those sales won't slow him down. Based on trading before the scandal, it's about 600 million shares every three months, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That's more than eight times the shares he holds in his own name. But only his own shares are easy to sell, and the insider-trading rules don't expire in February. The concern with hidden sales is that a former CEO might know bad news before the public does. Trading on that is still illegal, notice or no notice, and brokers keep records of every trade, which regulators can check. About 70 million shares, worth about $11 billion, are in Huang's own name, according to his SEC filings. The other 740 million or so, worth about $121 billion, sit in family trusts, including one he runs with his wife, Lori. That setup makes a quick fire sale hard. Even a full exit is smaller than it looks. His whole stake equals less than six days of typical Nvidia trading before the scandal, and Nvidia had $235 billion left on its buyback as of Sept. 28, enough to soak up every share he owns. Nvidia typically reports fourth quarter results and files its annual report in late February. That leaves a gap of about two weeks after Huang's insider period ends, and that has drawn attention online. Selling ahead of bad news he knew about would still be illegal. Leaving doesn't erase his signature, either. Huang signed off on Nvidia's financial statements every quarter as CEO, and the quarter it reports Tuesday ended Oct. 25, on his watch. That report will show whether Huang set up or canceled a preplanned trading plan before he left. "If you're Jensen and you're just sort of this megastar all the time, you know, you stop thinking that rules apply to you," Bradley Tusk, co-founder of Tusk Venture Partners, told Yahoo Finance on Friday. title: Nvidia's Ousted CEO Said a 1-Gigawatt Data Center Delay Costs $10 Billion a Quarter. Here's Why That Matters for Power Stocks. - The Motley Fool
content: Energy remains a critical bottleneck for AI growth. Former Nvidia (NVDA -2.01%) CEO Jensen Huang repeatedly warned the market about key bottlenecks to AI growth. And it's no wonder. As the world's largest supplier to the AI industry, Nvidia is not only reliant on long-term demand growth for AI technologies but also wants that growth runway to unfold as quickly and smoothly as possible. Last month, Huang quantified some of the lost economic potential when projects are delayed even just a few months. To be clear, Huang has come under scrutiny since he made these comments, for reasons completely unrelated to data center costs and Nvidia's potential. Nvidia's board is investigating reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation. Nvidia also issued a press release in which Huang admitted to an affair with a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. On Nov. 12, Huang resigned and is no longer CEO of Nvidia. But it doesn't diminish his expertise in discussing data center costs. A month ago, Huang outlined the total cost to construct a new 1 GW data center: roughly $50 billion. Such a facility, he claims, could generate around $40 billion in annual revenue. A three-month delay in construction, then, could result in $10 billion in lost revenue potential. Huang stressed how acutely aware the industry is of this lost economic potential, highlighting that "10 billion worth of revenues will make anybody anxious." There are many reasons why a data center could face delays. Nvidia is looking to clear up some construction hurdles by shifting more of the assembly process to the supply chain rather than on-site workers. This means more data center components will be able to enter operation faster, with fewer potential bottlenecks. Arguably, the biggest potential bottleneck for AI data construction in the long term, however, has nothing to do with on-site assembly. AI adoption rates are through the roof. Experts don't expect the pace of corporate and consumer adoption of AI technologies to slow for years to come. But as a report from McKinsey & Co. pointed out earlier this year, "there are real constraints on growth." Given how energy-intensive data centers are, bringing new energy capacity online will be critical to meeting rising end-market demand for AI technologies. "Incumbents can't meet demand for power," observes McKinsey & Co. The global consultancy isn't the only group concerned with AI's desperate need for more energy. "One of the clearest constraints on the AI build-out is energy," Morgan Stanley warns. "Power is emerging as the binding constraint of the AI build-out," J.P. Morgan adds. "A lack of capital is not the most pressing bottleneck for AI progress -- it's the power needed to fuel it," confirms Goldman Sachs. Without more power, the pace and scale of the data center build-out will almost certainly be constrained, costing AI companies heavily in lost revenue potential. How should investors position their portfolio with the AI industry's desperate need for more energy in mind? There are two approaches. The first is to expose your portfolio to next-gen energy companies such as NuScale Power (SMR -3.32%) and Oklo Inc. (OKLO -2.17%). These firms specialize in small modular reactors, or SMRs. At least in theory, SMRs can be built faster with lower upfront capital needs than conventional nuclear power plants. That's a benefit for AI companies looking to scale quickly and affordably. Only a handful of SMR systems have ever been successfully commercialized; however, this makes these stocks more of a high-risk, high-upside-potential investment. A more risk-conscious investment would be a company like Constellation Energy (CEG -0.78%) or Bloom Energy Corp. (BE -4.92%). Constellation is already one of the largest nuclear energy producers in the U.S. By expanding existing facilities and restarting older plants, It has significantly increased its ability to generate nuclear power, signing power purchase agreements with several major AI operators. Bloom, meanwhile, develops solid oxide fuel cell systems that convert natural gas, biogas, or hydrogen into electricity. These systems allow data centers to generate their own power, minimizing reliance on the grid. Sales growth is expected to exceed 100% this year, with economies of scale contributing to healthy profit growth. While most AI investors are focused on AI stocks, exposure to the AI economy can be gained at a lower premium by investing strategically in power stocks. A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company's recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon. The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Elon Musk wants Jensen Huang back in charge of Nvidia [NASDAQ: NVDA] — and he's putting his name on it. "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO [NASDAQ: TSLA] posted on X on Nov. 13. He isn't alone. As of 10:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 14, an online letter called Stand with Jensen listed more than 100,000 names — including more than 5,000 people who say they currently work at Nvidia. Huang co-founded the chipmaker in 1993 and led it for 33 years, building it into one of the world's most valuable companies. Nvidia announced Nov. 12 that he had resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. The board accepted his resignation Nov. 11, according to a regulatory filing. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and director Harvey Jones became the board's first-ever chair. His exit came after reports that he'd had extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect was recruited by China's top spy agency. Huang has admitted to an affair. Neither he nor Nvidia has been charged with any wrongdoing thus far. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change The Stand with Jensen letter asks the board to "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests." Beyond reinstatement, the letter asks the board to disclose the scope, independence and timeline of its investigation, give Huang a chance to respond before any final decision, and publicly explain the evidence behind his removal. The signers say they haven't been shown evidence that the woman at the center of the controversy was a spy, and argue Huang deserves "due process, not mob justice." The site says it isn't affiliated with Nvidia or Huang. Signers identify themselves, and organizers say they may hold new signatures for review before counting them. At this point, the site's live tracker broke the names down like this: Numbers are moving fast, and this is probably already out of date. For context, Nvidia had about 42,000 employees at the end of its last fiscal year in January, according to its annual report, so the self-identified current staff would represent roughly 12% of the company. Musk is listed at the top as a shareholder, alongside Replit CEO Amjad Masad; Gavin Baker, managing partner of Atreides Management; Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney; and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Cohere's Aidan Gomez and Serve Robotics CEO Ali Kashani are listed as partners. Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke replied "You have my sword" to Musk's petition post, though Moneywise didn't find his name on the list. Identities on the site are self-reported, and the list includes entries that appear to be fake or duplicated, including at least one offensive name listed as a current Nvidia employee. There's even an unverifiable entry for actress Sydney Sweeney listed as a shareholder. The totals are best read as a rough gauge of support rather than a true headcount. The pushback started inside the company. A longtime engineer posted to Nvidia's internal suggestion box urging the board to weigh employee sentiment before acting, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired. The post has drawn more than 1,600 comments, several asking the board to find a way to bring Huang back. One employee sent a companywide email demanding transparency about Huang's exit, writing: "I stand by Jensen." About two dozen employees posted support on LinkedIn, and Moneywise couldn't find any employee posts backing his departure. "Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," one employee told Wired. In an informal poll, we asked Moneywise followers whether Nvidia should bring Jensen back. Of 164 votes, 82% said "most definitely." Just 6% said "absolutely not," while 12% picked "he's poaching them all," a nod to the idea that Nvidia employees would follow Huang wherever he goes next. The post follows days of public support from Musk. On the night of Nov. 11, before Huang resigned, Musk replied "That would be an honor" to a ZeroHedge post urging him to hire Huang. The next day, he answered "True words" to AngelList co-founder Naval Ravikant, who wrote that "one does not just simply replace the founder," pointing to Steve Jobs and Travis Kalanick. When Ravikant followed up by calling Huang "the Steve Jobs of Nvidia" and "irreplaceable," Musk replied "True." He also replied "Always" to a post praising him for being a true friend to Huang. The two go back years. In May, Musk replied "True" to a repost of photos of the pair taken a decade apart, captioned "The most important thing in life is having true friends." Musk also has a business stake in the outcome. His rocket and AI company, SpaceX [NASDAQ: SPCX], has committed to building its AI data centers exclusively with Nvidia chips, and Nvidia owns a stake in SpaceX worth billions. The petition site also lists him as an Nvidia shareholder. Photos published by the Daily Mail show friends and family gathering at what the outlet described as his $38 million Pacific Heights mansion in San Francisco in the hours after he stepped down, as food deliveries, including bags of fried chicken, arrived at the door. Washington isn't done with him. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang agreed to come in. Three House committee chairs then asked him to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on Dec. 1, giving him until 8 p.m. ET on Nov. 13 to confirm or face a subpoena. It wasn't immediately clear whether Huang had confirmed in writing by the deadline. Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., has separately asked Huang to testify on Dec. 3. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whom Scott also called to testify, has agreed to appear. The petition's backers argue the board moved before the facts were in, and the central question is still open. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Nov. 12 there had been "no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice, or by me" about whether Alice Huang was a spy, according to Reuters. Beijing has denied that she is one, and President Donald Trump has said it isn't yet clear either way. What is on the record is narrower. Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said Nov. 12 that she has been barred from re-entering the country since February amid an investigation into possible offenses tied to Megaspeed, though it said that investigation did not concern espionage. There's recent precedent. In November 2023, OpenAI's board fired CEO Sam Altman, then reached a deal to bring him back about five days later after hundreds of employees threatened to quit. Even the White House has weighed in on both sides. President Donald Trump called Huang on Tuesday urging him to fight for his job, The New York Times reported. After Huang resigned, Trump posted on Truth Social that there was "only one man to take his place": Apple chairman Tim Cook. But the decision rests with Nvidia's board, and it has given no sign of reversing course. The company is continuing its own investigation into Huang, according to The Information. On Nov. 13, the board said it was still selecting a search firm for the CEO role and had not formally engaged any potential candidates, after the Financial Times reported that it had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas. Washington's scrutiny also goes beyond Huang himself: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has questioned whether Nvidia knew who it was selling chips to. Sam Altman came back within five days, so there's still time to see how this unfolds. The clock is ticking until Nvidia's Tuesday earnings call. Nvidia fell 8% to 9% in after-hours trading. If that holds, Nvidia will have lost about $600 billion of market value since Sunday. Then, just this morning, Bloomberg reported that Jensen Huang resigned. I want to explain what’s happened, why the board’s math changed overnight, and why Jensen matters so much to this company. Then I’ll talk about what it means for the business. Confirmed: Jensen admitted an affair in Sunday’s memo. “There is no excuse for what I did,” he wrote. He didn’t name the woman. Also confirmed: Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation, run by a committee of independent directors. It hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and former federal prosecutor Joon Kim. Before Sunday, Nvidia had described Jensen’s dealings with Alice Huang as normal business between a supplier and a customer’s executive. Jensen himself told Bloomberg last month that it was all “completely normal and not unusual.” Reported but not confirmed by Nvidia: That US intelligence concluded Alice Huang was working for China’s main spy agency. That her company, Megaspeed, may have helped move Nvidia chips into China. That Jensen had a second affair with a senior Nvidia executive. That the board is preparing to remove him. That it’s working with a search firm and considering a temporary CEO. China’s government calls the spy allegations a smear. It’s not going to admit anything, obviously. Megaspeed denies any wrongdoing. Nobody has been charged with anything. And as I write, Nvidia hasn’t commented on the board meeting. Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. Earlier this week, I would have told you the odds of the board firing Jensen were low. Here’s why… and why that’s no longer true. CEO scandals get a ton of attention, but they rarely cost CEOs their jobs. One firm that tracks CEO departures found that of nearly 3,000 CEO exits at Russell 3000 companies since January 2017, just 1.6% happened amid misconduct allegations. When boards do act, it’s almost never because of the affair itself. It’s because the CEO broke company rules or hid something from the board. McDonald’s fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019 over a relationship with an employee. It later recovered more than $100 million after accusing him of lying about other relationships. BP’s Bernard Looney resigned in 2023 after admitting he hadn’t been fully transparent with the board. Nestlé pushed out its CEO last year for failing to disclose a relationship with someone who reported to him. The pattern: A relationship with an employee and a failure to disclose are the triggers that push boards to act. Through Tuesday, the Jensen story didn’t fit that pattern. It was an affair with a customer’s top executive, who was allegedly acting in the interest of the Chinese Communist Party. That raised national security concerns and a possible conflict of interest, but the facts were still being investigated. A reported affair with a senior executive inside Nvidia is a different animal. Workplace relationships between a CEO and a subordinate in the company are the textbook case where boards say the rules leave them no choice. Add the company’s earlier insistence that the Alice Huang relationship was ordinary business, and you can see why the board’s math changed in one night. There’s the political side, too. Nvidia’s board was already under fire. It has no chairman. Several directors have served for decades. The law firm James Drury Partners ranked Nvidia’s corporate governance 609th among more than 650 big US companies. Plus, the board said it had “no reason to believe” anything was compromised before its own investigation even started. That guts its credibility. Directors who’ve been criticized for deferring to a founder (whether deserved or not) now have every reason to show they won’t. That’s my read, not something they’ve said. But I’d bet that was being discussed before Jensen made the decision for the board. All of this sits on top of a national security story that hasn’t gone away. Nvidia’s best chips are the closest thing the US has to a strategic weapon in the AI race. That’s why the US bans exporting the most advanced ones to China. Jensen has been one of the president’s most trusted AI advisers, and he’s lobbied hard to loosen those rules. Doing that while in a close relationship with someone US officials believe reported to Chinese intelligence is a counterintelligence nightmare, even if nothing was ever compromised. The Justice Department is reportedly leading several investigations involving Alice Huang. House committees asked Jensen to brief them in private on November 18. That’s the same day Trump is scheduled to meet Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, where chip access is one of the hottest topics. Meanwhile, Congress is weighing tougher chip export rules in the big annual defense bill. Whatever the board might have decided, that pressure isn’t going away anytime soon. To really get why this matters so much for investors, we need to talk about how unusual Jensen’s role is. “Key-man risk” is a simple idea. A company depends so heavily on one person that losing them would seriously hurt the business. In my opinion, aside from the companies run by Elon Musk, Nvidia has more of it than any company in the world. title: Nvidia Stock Braces For AI Chipmaker's First Report Without Jensen Huang - Investor's Business Daily
content:
BREAKING: Futures Waver As Jensen Huang Reportedly Mulls Nvidia Return Nvidia (NVDA) will report its fiscal third-quarter earnings late Tuesday following a headline-grabbing scandal that saw co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang resign in disgrace. Nvidia stock has slumped since the allegations first leaked. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer, will lead the earnings call for analysts. Nvidia investors will be curious if Ian Buck will be on the call. Buck, Nvidia's vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing, has emerged as a leading internal candidate to replace Huang. Wall Street analysts assume a beat-and-raise report is in the cards for Nvidia's Q3 and likely will focus on a future without its rockstar co-founder and artificial intelligence champion. Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member on Thursday after the embarrassing disclosure of two extramarital affairs — one with a subordinate and the other with a reputed Chinese spy. The board of directors is conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates. Arm Holdings (ARM) CEO Rene Haas, who previously worked at Nvidia, has been named as a possible replacement for Huang, according to the Financial Times. Nvidia stock plummeted to its lowest level since June 2025 after the CEO change before recovering somewhat as many investors surmised a bottom for the AI leader. But on Friday, Nvidia stock fell again. On the stock market today, Nvidia stock retreated 3% to close at 162.85. Analysts polled by FactSet expect Nvidia to earn an adjusted $2.47 a share, up 90% year over year, on sales of $108.7 billion, up 91%, in its fiscal Q3 ended Oct. 25. For Nvidia's fiscal Q4, FactSet estimates point to the company earning an adjusted $2.74 a share, up 69% year over year, on sales of $124.8 billion, up 83%. However, some analysts have speculated that the AI chipmaker might give cautious guidance, given the upheaval in the C-suite. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that CFO Kress clashed with Huang over his aggressive "circular financing" deals. Under those arrangements, Nvidia provides financing for neoclouds and other companies and that money comes back to Nvidia in the form of semiconductor purchases. Wall Street analysts have expressed worries about Nvidia's financial exposure in the AI data center boom. "This expansion into neoclouds/data centers has forced Nvidia to pivot from a pure chipmaker into an industry financier, exposing its balance sheet to significant credit and real estate risks," Daniel Morgan, senior portfolio manager at Synovus Trust, said in a report. Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, concurred. "The biggest potential risk that we have to look at here is the hundreds of billions of dollars of financing deals that use chips as collateral is at stake," Malek said in a report. "Nvidia is at the center of a very complex web of financing." And the next Nvidia CEO might be more risk-averse, Malek said. Nvidia's problems aren't over after Huang's replacement. The U.S. government is investigating whether his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, facilitated the diversion of Nvidia AI chips into China. And the U.S. will want to know if Kress and other executives were aware of illegal shipments of graphics processing units to China. Meanwhile, Wall Street analysts continue to bail on Nvidia stock. HSBC and GF Securities on Friday downgraded Nvidia stock to hold from buy. Further, Barclays and Rosenblatt Securities added to the long list of investment firms that have cut their price targets on Nvidia stock this week. Nvidia's CEO change is a near-term overhang on its stock, analysts say. But the company's product road map is well established for the next couple of years. "Nvidia's product road map is likely firmly set through at least 2028-2029 and (we) do not believe a new CEO can/will change the road map over the next 2-3 years," Needham analyst Quinn Bolton said in a report Thursday. He rates Nvidia stock as buy with a price target of 200. Raymond James analyst Simon Leopold said the market's reaction to Huang's departure suggests that Nvidia is a "one-man band." "While Jensen Huang has been a standout CEO closely associated with the company, we argue that Nvidia is more than just its CEO," Leopold said in a report Thursday. "The AI evolution continues and Nvidia remains an important player." Follow Patrick Seitz on X at @IBD_PSeitz for more stories on consumer technology, software and semiconductor stocks. title: Breakfast News: What NVDA’s CEO Exit Means for You - The Motley Fool
content: Huang built a company with the products, people, and customers to outlast him, and we expect Nvidia to come through this. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's (NVDA -2.01%) chief executive amid controversies over his personal conduct and questions about whether Nvidia's chips reached China through a customer in Singapore. His exit followed a week of reports about his personal life. The first concerned an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's customers in Singapore. U.S. officials suspected the executive of spying for China, which China denied. On Wednesday, a second relationship, with one of Huang's direct reports, came to light. The board met that night, and the company announced Huang's resignation the following morning. We think investors are right to take Huang's departure seriously. In our view, though, the sell-off prices in more damage than the business has shown so far. If you've followed Nvidia for any length of time, you know how central Huang has been. He co-founded the company in 1993 and led it for all 33 years. His leadership structure was also known for being unusually flat, as he had 33 direct reports at last count, according to CNBC. Huang pushed Nvidia as an innovator and technologist. He launched CUDA (software that lets developers program Nvidia's chips) in 2006 and boldly committed the company to artificial intelligence (AI) computing long before it became a mainstream market. He also managed Nvidia's largest customer relationships himself and represented the company in Washington on export rules for China. That is a lot for one person to hand off, let alone overnight, and Nvidia has no named successor to take it on. For now, CFO Colette Kress, who has worked alongside Huang since 2013 and has joined him on every earnings call, will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,116,882 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. We understand why the market reacted so sharply. A company that leaned this heavily on one person's judgment now has to make its next big decisions without him, and under federal scrutiny. Analyst Dan Ives estimates Nvidia is worth 25% to 30% less without Huang, and some discount is warranted. With shares dropping to $148.80 in Thursday trading and closing at around $166, the market has already applied much of it. What reassures us is that Huang's exit on its own is unlikely to change Nvidia's revenue much over the next two years. Demand for its chips is still growing quickly. Last quarter, revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, and the company guided to $108 billion for the quarter that ended in October. By any measure, that's a business in good health. Chips take years to design, so the products Nvidia will sell through 2027 were planned while Huang was still in charge, and customers have already ordered many of them. Even if regulators cut off sales routed through Singapore, we estimate Nvidia would lose no more than about 5% of its revenue. A broader crackdown would cost more, and the investigations will help decide whether one comes.
